title: How the Iran War Is Rewiring the Oil Market
summary: Bloomberg explainer on why the Hormuz closure caused a smaller oil spike than feared: stock releases, bypass pipelines and Chinese import cuts.

assertions.quote: Existing surplus, strategic national reserves, and commercial inventory offset nine million of that.

verdicts.note: Coordinated IEA stock releases, Saudi and UAE pipeline bypasses and a sharp drop in Chinese crude imports replaced much of the lost flow; prices peaked far below the $150-200 bank forecasts.

A large spike did occur: WTI rose 58% from 64.51 (Feb 2026) to 102.13 (May 2026) and was back at 97.31 in Sep, though it stayed below the Jun 2022 peak of 114.84 and the 2008 high of 133.88; the series cannot tell whether reserves, pipelines or Chinese import cuts capped it.

assertions.quote: in relative terms, the West has been cushioned from the spike compared to some of the poorer nations

verdicts.note: US and Atlantic-basin supply is not routed through Hormuz, and SPR releases plus record exports added barrels, so Asian importers faced the tighter market.

assertions.quote: you won't necessarily need as many ships to go through Hormuz in the long term

verdicts.note: Prediction; Gulf producers are expanding pipeline capacity but most Gulf export volume still has no alternative outlet.

assertions.quote: Solar and oil don't really compete with each other because very little oil is used in the power sector.
